text.p: Dissidents from Cambodia's royalist FUNCINPEC party on Sunday voted to "expel" as party leader First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, who shrugged off the rebels' move as meaningless.

The dissident faction, which has the support of Ranariddh's co-premier and political rival Hun Sen, elected a provincial governor, Toan Chay, as president of the party in a step likely to prolong a feud in the coalition government which has paralysed parliament for weeks.
FUNCINPEC expelled eight dissident members of parliament from the party last month but they refused to accept their expulsion and instead called the Sunday meeting.
"These people they are already outside the party," FUNCINPEC Secretary General Loy Sim Chheang told Reuters. "He (Ranariddh) doesn't think about this because they are not FUNCINPEC members."
Ranariddh has demanded that the eight dissident members of parliament be expelled from parliament but Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party and its allies have blocked the move.
Cambodia's problem-plagued coalition was formed in 1993 after United Nations-supervised elections in which Ranariddh's party won 58 seats in the 120-seat assembly, against 51 for Hun Sen's party.
Ranariddh said last week that the national assembly should be dissolved if the deadlock over the royalist dissidents could not be resolved.
In a separate development, Cambodia's Khmer Rouge guerrilla group said on Sunday that elections had begun in their remote zone of control in the north of the country.

The radical guerrilla group, which boycotted a 1993 general election organised by the United Nations, said in a radio broadcast monitored in Phnom Penh that the local elections could take up to five months in areas where they and government forces vie for control.

The Khmer Rouge split last year, a more moderate faction based in the west of the country striking a ceasefire deal with the government while hardliners, under the control of the notorious Pol Pot, remained in their jungle bases in Cambodia's far north.
Political analysts in Phnom Penh said the guerrilla group was trying to present a more democratic face in the run-up to a general election next year.
Nominal Khmer Rouge leader Khieu Samphan, who is with the hardline faction, said in a guerrilla radio broadcast last month that he would support an alliance formed by Ranariddh.
